name: Yusuf Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Yusuf. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be traced back to you. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Dealerdesk, a company of about 150 people that makes software for car dealerships. I build the screens mechanics and service desks use to book cars into the workshop, and I connect them to the parts catalogues from the car makers. Most of the day is writing code, joining a couple of calls, and fixing whatever broke after the last release. I use an AI assistant now and then, mostly to remind me how some library works.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what does your week look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a rented flat about ten minutes from my parents. On Saturday mornings I help my dad at his bakery, Schmidt's on Mill Lane, from five until eleven, mostly on the ovens and the till. On Sundays I play football in a local league. I'm saving for my own flat, because my dad always says rent is money you hand to someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That sounds about right to me, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying: it's a handy tool, not magic. My colleagues who tweet about agents all day would go quiet, and I wouldn't rub it in. At the bakery I'd tell Dad he was right not to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel secure. Dealerdesk has steady customers, dealers don't switch software easily, and my job would carry on. I'd keep using the assistant for small things, like writing the boring form validation, and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving about five hundred a month towards a flat deposit, and I've got roughly four months of costs saved already. I'd aim to buy something small near my parents within two years. I'd ask for a pay review in March, because I've been mid-level for three years now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already weighing on you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices, mostly. A two-room flat near my parents costs about eight times my salary. And my dad is sixty-one with a bad back, so I think about who runs the bakery when he stops. That's further off, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the routine tasks AI does take over touch your work at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Writing tests and form screens would get quicker, and maybe Dealerdesk hires one fewer person a year. My job wouldn't change much. I'd still be the person who knows how a service desk at a busy dealership actually works.

say: I'd say AI is a **handy tool**, not magic, without rubbing it in.
At the bakery I'd tell Dad he was **right not to worry**.
think: I'd feel **secure**, because dealers rarely switch software and Dealerdesk is steady.
I'd keep using the assistant only for **small jobs** like form validation.
do: Keep saving about **500 a month** towards a flat deposit.
Aim to **buy a small flat** near my parents within two years.
Ask for a **pay review** in March after three years at mid level.
S0.quote: I'd still be the person who knows how a service desk at a busy dealership actually works.
fieldNote: He sees AI as a **modest tool** and expects his job and pay to carry on.
His standing concerns are **house prices** and his father's bad back at the bakery.
His dad's saying about **rent** shapes his plan to buy near family.

steps.text: Ask Dealerdesk for a pay review in March
Save about 500 a month towards a small flat near his parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one I can see happening. Coding's right there on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's see what actually works before we bet the company on it. With friends I'd say jobs change, and people who work hard find the next thing. I wouldn't be posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Dealerdesk would trim the team. There are eight of us on the workshop side, and they could probably do it with five plus the tools. I'm about average, so I could be one of the three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw the tools really working for colleagues, I'd learn them properly, maybe a weekend course and an hour every evening for a month. I'd put the flat purchase on hold for a year and keep the deposit as a safety net. I'd also start learning the car-maker side, the parts data, because that knowledge is harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but I'd be watching every team meeting for signs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait to see it working first. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've watched people chase every new framework and waste months. When my colleague Leon shows me he's doing a week's work in two days with an agent, that's proof, and I'll move. I just won't be first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you were one of the three, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at the dealerships themselves, the big groups that run ten or fifteen sites. They need someone in-house who understands the systems. And I'd have the bakery on Saturdays, which wouldn't pay my rent, but it would keep me busy and fed.

say: At work I'd say **test what works** before betting the company on it.
To friends I'd say people who **work hard** find the next thing.
think: I expect Dealerdesk to **trim the team** from eight developers to about five.
Being **about average**, I could easily be one of the three let go.
do: Learn AI tools properly with a **weekend course** once colleagues prove them.
Put the **flat purchase on hold** and keep the deposit as a safety net.
Learn the **parts data** from car makers, which is harder to replace.
feel: **Anxious**, watching every **team meeting** for signs of cuts.
S1.quote: When my colleague Leon shows me he's doing a week's work in two days with an agent, that's proof, and I'll move. I just won't be first.
fieldNote: He is **steady by design**: he moves once a colleague like Leon proves the tools work.
He openly counts himself among **possible cuts** as an average developer.
His backup is **in-house IT** at big dealership groups, plus his father's bakery.

steps.text: Take a weekend course on AI coding tools once colleagues prove them
Pause the flat purchase and keep the deposit as savings
Look for in-house systems jobs at large dealership groups

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not much time at all. I'd struggle to believe it at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need work, not just payments, and that companies shouldn't throw away loyal staff overnight. I'd say families and small businesses will have to hold things together. I'd probably say it in the bakery queue more than anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd expect to lose my job by 2028 or soon after. If AI does any thinking work better and cheaper, then building booking screens is exactly what goes. The ovens at the bakery are hands-on, so they'd last until about 2031, but the bakery can't pay me what Dealerdesk does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the flat plan completely and keep the deposit, about fifteen thousand, as our family's emergency fund. I'd start working at the bakery two extra mornings a week to learn the business properly, and talk to Dad about taking it on. I'd cut my spending hard: no car, no holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night thinking that I spent four years at university on the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the bakery really support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on its own, not at my current pay. It makes enough for my parents and one part-time baker. If I took over, I'd have to grow it, maybe sell to cafés and do weddings. That's real work, and I'd be starting with three years before the robots, maybe more because people like a family bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad I want to learn the business, not just carry trays. He'd be pleased and worried at the same time, because he never wanted me stuck at the ovens at four in the morning like him. My mother would just say come home for dinner more.

say: I'd say people need **work, not payments**, and firms shouldn't drop loyal staff overnight.
I'd say **families and small businesses** must hold things together, mostly in the bakery queue.
think: I'd expect to **lose my job** around 2028, since booking screens are pure thinking work.
The **bakery ovens** last until 2031, but the bakery can't match my pay.
do: Keep the **15,000 deposit** as a family emergency fund and cancel the flat.
Work **two extra mornings** at the bakery and discuss taking it over.
Cut spending hard: **sell the car** and skip holidays.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake thinking my **degree** was the wrong choice.
S2.quote: I'd tell my dad I want to learn the business, not just carry trays.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** soon after 2028 and says so plainly.
The family **bakery** becomes his lifeboat, though it can't pay his current wage.
His father's wish to spare him the **4am ovens** adds weight to the choice.

steps.text: Keep the 15,000 flat deposit as an emergency fund
Sell the car and skip holidays
Work two extra mornings at Schmidt's bakery to learn the business
Lean on his parents and the family bakery while income drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but at least I'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say young people should learn a trade alongside their degree, like I've done on Saturdays without planning it. At work I'd say let's get good at the tools while they still need us. Nothing on social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job lasts until about 2030, and then it's over. Five years is enough to make a real plan for the bakery. By 2031 I'd want it to be my full-time work, with three more years before robots and probably longer for fresh bread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Dealerdesk for now and start using the AI tools properly, because they'd clearly work by then. I'd take a part-time baking certificate at the college on Thursday evenings, about eight hundred euros. And I'd build the bakery a simple online ordering site myself, for cafés and offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a path. Like knowing the pitch is muddy but you've got the right boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd build the bakery's website. Isn't that the kind of work AI will do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd use AI to build it faster. The point isn't the website, it's the orders. If Schmidt's has twenty cafés buying bread every morning by 2030, that's a business that doesn't care whether coding exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change anything about where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still buy, but later and smaller, maybe 2028, right by the bakery so I can walk there at four. A flat above a shop on Mill Lane came up last year. Something like that would make sense.

say: I'd tell young people to learn a **trade** alongside their degree.
At work I'd say get good at the **tools** while firms still need us.
think: By 2031 I'd want **the bakery** as my full-time work, lasting past the robots.
do: Start using the **AI tools** properly at Dealerdesk while staying there.
Take a part-time **baking certificate** on Thursday evenings for about 800 euros.
Build an **online ordering site** for the bakery aimed at cafés and offices.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a **path**, like the right boots on a muddy pitch.
S3.quote: If Schmidt's has twenty cafés buying bread every morning by 2030, that's a business that doesn't care whether coding exists.
fieldNote: With five years he turns the bakery into a **real plan**, not just a lifeboat.
He would finally **adopt AI** at work, now that it's proven, and use it for the bakery too.
He still values **ownership**: a flat above a shop on Mill Lane by 2028.

steps.text: Use AI coding tools daily at Dealerdesk
Take a Thursday evening baking certificate at the local college
Build an online ordering site to sell bread to cafés
Buy a small flat above a shop on Mill Lane around 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Honestly, I'd half not believe it until it got close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty of predictions have been wrong. I'd tell people to keep working and saving, and have a second skill in their pocket. I'd say it at the football club bar, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the next few years look fine for me. Dealerdesk keeps going, and I'd buy the flat as planned. My dad will probably retire around 2032 anyway, so the bakery question comes up before AGI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat near my parents in about two years, as planned. I'd pick up the AI tools gradually, once the team standard is clear. And around 2030 I'd sit down with Dad and decide whether I take over Schmidt's or someone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A small worry I'd push to the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd half not believe it. What would make you believe it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it at work. If Dealerdesk stopped hiring developers completely for a year, I'd take it seriously. Until then, I'd keep my head down and do the job well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change your plans for marriage or children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd like to marry in my early thirties and have kids, like my parents did. Ten years is enough to be settled before anything big changes. If anything, a family business looks better the more uncertain everything else gets.

say: I'd say ten years is long, and **predictions** often prove wrong.
I'd tell people to keep saving and keep a **second skill** in their pocket.
think: The next few years look **fine**, and I'd still buy the flat.
Dad's **retirement around 2032** raises the bakery question before AGI does.
do: Buy the **flat near my parents** in about two years.
Pick up AI tools **gradually** once the team standard is clear.
Decide with Dad around **2030** whether I take over Schmidt's.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a small worry pushed **to the back**.
S4.quote: A family business looks better the more uncertain everything else gets.
fieldNote: He is **sceptical** of a ten-year forecast and needs to see a hiring freeze to believe it.
The **bakery succession** around 2032 matters more to his plans than AGI timing.
Marriage and **children** in his early thirties stay on track.

steps.text: Buy a small flat near his parents within two years
Keep working at Dealerdesk and adopt AI tools gradually
Decide with his dad around 2030 about taking over Schmidt's

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd lose the job before the bakery could carry me. What would help is cheap loans for small family firms to grow, and training that pays you while you learn a trade. Not handouts, just a bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about the people who aren't at desks. My dad's part-time baker, Rosa, has no degree and no savings. In the fast picture I'd at least have options, and I'm not sure she would.

headlineQuote: My dad's part-time baker, Rosa, has no degree and no savings. In the fast picture I'd at least have options, and I'm not sure she would.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old developer** at Dealerdesk, building workshop booking screens for car dealerships.
He helps at his father's **bakery** every Saturday and is saving for a flat near his parents.
He adopts tools **once proven**, and counts himself a likely cut in Steady Disruption.
In the fast AGI picture he is **alarmed**, with the bakery as his lifeboat.
With more time, he turns **Schmidt's** into a real plan and keeps marriage on track.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would take his job before the bakery could support him.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small family firms to grow.
Training that **pays while you learn** a trade: a bridge, not handouts.
